arXiv:2103.00969v4 [math.AP] 21 Feb 2025

On a damped nonlinear beam equation

David Raske Email address: nonlinear.problem.solver@gmail.com
Abstract.

In this note we analyze the large time behavior of solutions to an initial/boundary problem involving a damped nonlinear beam equation. We show that under physically realistic conditions on the nonlinear terms in the equation of motion the energy is a decreasing function of time and solutions converge to a stationary solution with respect to a desirable norm.

Key words and phrases: 
nonlinear beam equation; elliptic boundary value problem; suspension bridges
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary 35L35; Secondary 35Q99, 35L76

1. Introduction

Let aa, bb be two real numbers. Let TT be a positive real number. Let F1F_{1} and F2F_{2} be two functions from ℝ\mathbb{R} into ℝ\mathbb{R}. Let ff be a map from [0,T][0,T] into L2​(a,b)L^{2}(a,b) Initial/boundary value problems of the form

(1.1) m​ut​t+σ​ux​x​x​x+F1​(ut)+F2​(u)=f⁡(x,t), on ​(a,b)×(0,T)u⁡(a,t)=0=u⁡(b,t), for all ​t​ in ​(0,T)ux​x​(a,t)=0=ux​x​(b,t), for all ​t​ in ​(0,T)u(x,0)=u0(x),ut(x,0)=u1(x) for all x in (a,b).\begin{split}&mu_{tt}+\sigma u_{xxxx}+F_{1}(u_{t})+F_{2}(u)=f(x,t),\text{ on }(a,b)\times(0,T)\\ &u(a,t)=0=u(b,t),\text{ for all }t\text{ in }(0,T)\\ &u_{xx}(a,t)=0=u_{xx}(b,t),\text{ for all }t\text{ in }(0,T)\\ &u(x,0)=u_{0}(x),u_{t}(x,0)=u_{1}(x)\text{ for all }x\text{ in }(a,b).\\ \end{split}

arise naturally in the study of vibrations in slender beams. In particular, they have been used to model vibrations in suspension bridges and railroad tracks. A treatment of the existence and uniqueness problem of the above can be found in [2].

Before we continue we need to define some spaces. Let Ω:=(a,b)\Omega:=(a,b), and let H∗2​(Ω)H^{2}_{*}(\Omega) be the intersection of H01​(Ω)H^{1}_{0}(\Omega) with H2​(Ω)H^{2}(\Omega). It is equipped with the inner-product

(1.2) (u,v)H∗2=∫Ωux​x​vx​x​𝑑x.(u,v)_{H^{2}_{*}}=\int_{\Omega}u_{xx}v_{xx}dx.

Let H∗4​(Ω)H^{4}_{*}(\Omega) be the elements uu of H4​(Ω)H^{4}(\Omega) such that u∈H∗2​(Ω)u\in H^{2}_{*}(\Omega) and ux​x∈H∗2​(Ω)u_{xx}\in H^{2}_{*}(\Omega); it is equipped with the inner-product

(1.3) (u,v)H∗4=∫Ωux​x​x​x​vx​x​x​x​𝑑x.(u,v)_{H^{4}_{*}}=\int_{\Omega}u_{xxxx}v_{xxxx}dx.

In [2] it is shown that the above inner-products make H∗2​(Ω)H^{2}_{*}(\Omega) and H∗4​(Ω)H^{4}_{*}(\Omega) Hilbert spaces.

Now, suppose there exists a function u:[0,T]→L2​((a,b))u:[0,T]\rightarrow L^{2}((a,b)) such that u∈C0​([0,T],H04​((a,b)))u\in C^{0}([0,T],H^{4}_{0}((a,b))), u∈C1​([0,T],H02​((a,b)))u\in C^{1}([0,T],H^{2}_{0}((a,b))), u∈C2​([0,T],L2​((a,b)))u\in C^{2}([0,T],L^{2}((a,b))), u⁡(0)=u0u(0)=u_{0}, u′​(0)=u1u^{\prime}(0)=u_{1}, and such that for all ϕ∈Cc∞​(0,T)\phi\in C^{\infty}_{c}(0,T) and v∈L2​((,,,))v\in L^{2}((a,b)) we have

(1.4) ∫0Tm​(u′′,v)L2​ϕ​(t)​𝑑t=−∫0T[σ(ux​x​x​x,v)L2+(F1(u′),v)L2+(F2(u),v)L2−(f(x,t),v)L2]ϕ(t)dt.\begin{split}&\int_{0}^{T}m(u^{\prime\prime},v)_{L^{2}}\phi(t)\,dt\\ &=-\int_{0}^{T}[\sigma(u_{xxxx},v)_{L^{2}}+(F_{1}(u^{\prime}),v)_{L^{2}}+(F_{2}(u),v)_{L^{2}}-(f(x,t),v)_{L^{2}}]\phi(t)\,dt.\end{split}

We will then call uu a pseudo classical solution of (1.1).

Now, suppose there exists a function u:[0,∞)→L2​((a,b))u:[0,\infty)\rightarrow L^{2}((a,b)) such that u∈C0​([0,∞),H04​((a,b)))u\in C^{0}([0,\infty),H^{4}_{0}((a,b))), u∈C1​([0,∞),H02​((a,b)))u\in C^{1}([0,\infty),H^{2}_{0}((a,b))), u∈C2​([0,∞),L2​((a,b)))u\in C^{2}([0,\infty),L^{2}((a,b))), u⁡(0)=u0u(0)=u_{0}, u′​(0)=u1u^{\prime}(0)=u_{1}, and such that for all ϕ∈Cc∞​(0,∞)\phi\in C^{\infty}_{c}(0,\infty) and v∈L2​((,,,))v\in L^{2}((a,b)) we have

We will then call uu a global pseudo classical solution of the initial/boundary value problem

(1.6) m​ut​t+σ​ux​x​x​x+F1​(ut)+F2​(u)=f⁡(x,t), on ​(a,b)×(0,∞)u⁡(a,t)=0=u⁡(b,t), for all ​t​ in ​(0,∞)ux​x​(a,t)=0=ux​x​(b,t), for all ​t​ in ​(0,∞)u(x,0)=u0(x),ut(x,0)=u1(x) for all x in (a,b).\begin{split}&mu_{tt}+\sigma u_{xxxx}+F_{1}(u_{t})+F_{2}(u)=f(x,t),\text{ on }(a,b)\times(0,\infty)\\ &u(a,t)=0=u(b,t),\text{ for all }t\text{ in }(0,\infty)\\ &u_{xx}(a,t)=0=u_{xx}(b,t),\text{ for all }t\text{ in }(0,\infty)\\ &u(x,0)=u_{0}(x),u_{t}(x,0)=u_{1}(x)\text{ for all }x\text{ in }(a,b).\\ \end{split}

A natural question to ask if a global pseudo classical solution exists is whether or not it converges to a solution of the boundary value problem

(1.7) σ​ux​x​x​x+F2​(u)=f⁡(x)​ on ​(a,b),u⁡(a)=0=u⁡(b),ux​x​(a)=0=ux​x​(b).\begin{split}&\sigma u_{xxxx}+F_{2}(u)=f(x)\text{ on }(a,b),\\ &u(a)=0=u(b),\\ &u_{xx}(a)=0=u_{xx}(b).\\ \end{split}

as t→∞t\rightarrow\infty. Since (1.1) is derived from a damped mechanical problem, it’s also natural to ask whether or not the total energy is decreasing or not if ff is independent of time. These two questions are the focus of this paper, and the main result is

Theorem 1.1.

Let aa and bb be two real numbers, with a<ba<b. Let mm, σ\sigma, and cc be three positive real numbers. Let dd be a non-negative real number. Let Ω\Omega be the open interval (a,b)(a,b). Let ff be a C1C^{1} map from [0,∞)[0,\infty) into L2​(Ω)L^{2}(\Omega) that is independent of t∈[0,∞)t\in[0,\infty). Let F1:ℝ→ℝF_{1}:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} be defined as follows: If we write F1=F1​(x)F_{1}=F_{1}(x), then F1​(x)=c​x+d​|x|​xF_{1}(x)=cx+d|x|x. Let F2:ℝ→ℝF_{2}:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} be a continuously differentiable function such that F2F_{2} is non-decreasing and such that there exists a real number rr such that F2​(r)=0F_{2}(r)=0. Furthermore, let u0u_{0} be an element of H∗4​(Ω)H_{*}^{4}(\Omega) and let u1u_{1} be an element of H∗2​(Ω)H^{2}_{*}(\Omega). Suppose (1.6) possesses a unique global pseudo classical solution, uu. Then, this solution satisfies u⁡(t)→u^u(t)\rightarrow\hat{u} in H∗2​(Ω)H^{2}_{*}(\Omega) and u′​(t)→0u^{\prime}(t)\rightarrow 0 in L2​(Ω)L^{2}(\Omega), where u^\hat{u} is the unique solution of the boundary value problem (1.7).

Here we restrict our attention to the nonlinear damping term, F1​(ut)=c​ut+d​|ut|​utF_{1}(u_{t})=cu_{t}+d|u_{t}|u_{t}, because it is thought to provide a realistic model of damping, but is simple enough to result in a tractable problem. The linear term dominates when |ut||u_{t}| is small, but |F1​(ut)||F_{1}(u_{t})| grows like d​(ut)2d(u_{t})^{2} as |ut|→∞|u_{t}|\rightarrow\infty. This seems to be more realistic than just F1​(ut)=c​utF_{1}(u_{t})=cu_{t} or F1​(ut)=d​|ut|​utF_{1}(u_{t})=d|u_{t}|u_{t}.

In section two of this paper we make some observations about how global pseudo classical solutions of (1.1) evolve as t→∞t\rightarrow\infty, for general damping terms F1F_{1}. In section three of this paper we use these observations to prove Theorem 1.2.

Finally, it should be noted that Theorem 1.2 holds with F1​(x)=a​x+b​|x|p−2​xF_{1}(x)=ax+b|x|^{p-2}x, where aa and bb are a positive real numbers and where pp is a positive real number greater than or equal to 22 in value. It should also be noted that the results of Theorem 1.1 hold for a much broader range of elliptic differential operators and boundary conditions that the ones used here. We restrict our attention to the one dimensional bi-Laplacian augmented with homogeneous Navier boundary conditions, because the author is interested in bending phenomena and does not want to distract attention away from the nonlinear terms in the equation of motion.

2. Preliminaries

The goal of this section is to make some useful observations about how solutions of (1.1) evolve with respect to time, especially when ff is independent of tt. So let TT, mm, and σ\sigma be positive real numbers, and let aa and bb be two real numbers with a<ba<b. Let Ω\Omega be the interval (a,b)(a,b). Let F1:ℝ→ℝF_{1}:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} be a non-decreasing C1C^{1} function such that F1​(0)=0F_{1}(0)=0. Let f∈C1​([0,∞),L2​(Ω))f\in C^{1}([0,\infty);L^{2}(\Omega)). Finally, let u0∈H∗4​(Ω)u_{0}\in H^{4}_{*}(\Omega) and let u1∈H∗2​(Ω)u_{1}\in H^{2}_{*}(\Omega).

Now suppose that (1.1) has a unique pseudo classical solution uTu_{T}. It follows that for all v∈H∗2​(Ω)v\in H^{2}_{*}(\Omega) we have

(2.1) m⁡<uT′′​(t),v>+(F1​(uT′​(t),v)L2+σ​(uT​(t),v)H∗2+(F2​(uT​(t)),v)L2CLOSE=(f⁡(t),v)L2,\begin{split}&m<u_{T}^{\prime\prime}(t),v>+(F_{1}(u_{T}^{\prime}(t),v)_{L^{2}}+\sigma(u_{T}(t),v)_{H^{2}_{*}}+(F_{2}(u_{T}(t)),v)_{L^{2}}\\ &=(f(t),v)_{L^{2}},\end{split}

for all t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T]. This, in turn, allows us to write

(2.2) m⁡<uT′​(t),uT′​(t)>+(F1​(uT′​(t),uT′​(t))L2+σ​(uT​(t),uT′​(t))H∗2+CLOSE(F2​(uT​(t)),uT′​(t))L2=(f⁡(t),uT′​(t))L2,\begin{split}&m<u_{T}^{\prime}(t),u_{T}^{\prime}(t)>+(F_{1}(u_{T}^{\prime}(t),u_{T}^{\prime}(t))_{L^{2}}+\sigma(u_{T}(t),u_{T}^{\prime}(t))_{H^{2}_{*}}+\\ &(F_{2}(u_{T}(t)),u_{T}^{\prime}(t))_{L^{2}}=(f(t),u_{T}^{\prime}(t))_{L^{2}},\end{split}

for almost every t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T]. Since uT​(t)u_{T}(t) is a pseudo classical solution of (1.1) all of the above terms are summable. It follows that we can integrate all of them from 00 to tt, where 0≤t≤T0\leq t\leq T. This leaves us with

(2.3) ∫0t(m⁡<uT′′​(s),uT′​(s)>+(F1​(uT′​(s),uT′​(s))L2+σ​(uT​(s),uT′​(s))H∗2+CLOSECLOSEOPEN(F2​(uT​(s)),uT′​(s))L2)​ds=∫0t(f⁡(s),uT′​(s))L2​ds,\begin{split}&\int_{0}^{t}(m<u_{T}^{\prime\prime}(s),u_{T}^{\prime}(s)>+(F_{1}(u_{T}^{\prime}(s),u_{T}^{\prime}(s))_{L^{2}}+\sigma(u_{T}(s),u_{T}^{\prime}(s))_{H^{2}_{*}}+\\ &(F_{2}(u_{T}(s)),u^{\prime}_{T}(s))_{L^{2}})ds=\int_{0}^{t}(f(s),u_{T}^{\prime}(s))_{L^{2}}ds,\end{split}

for all t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T]. It follows that

(2.4) ∫0t(m​12​dd​s​(uT′​(s),uT′​(s))L2+(F1​(uT′​(s)),uT′​(s))L2+σ​12​dd​s​(uT​(s),uT​(s))H∗2+CLOSEOPEN(F2​(uT​(s)),uT′​(s))L2)​ds=∫0t(f⁡(s),uT′​(s))L2​ds,\begin{split}&\int_{0}^{t}(m\frac{1}{2}\frac{d}{ds}(u_{T}^{\prime}(s),u_{T}^{\prime}(s))_{L^{2}}+(F_{1}(u_{T}^{\prime}(s)),u_{T}^{\prime}(s))_{L^{2}}+\sigma\frac{1}{2}\frac{d}{ds}(u_{T}(s),u_{T}(s))_{H^{2}_{*}}+\\ &(F_{2}(u_{T}(s)),u_{T}^{\prime}(s))_{L^{2}})ds=\int_{0}^{t}(f(s),u_{T}^{\prime}(s))_{L^{2}}ds,\end{split}

for all t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T]. Let VV be a function from H∗2​(Ω)H^{2}_{*}(\Omega) into the real numbers such that V⁡(u)=∫Ωf2​(u⁡(x))​𝑑xV(u)=\int_{\Omega}f_{2}(u(x))dx for all u∈H∗2​(Ω)u\in H^{2}_{*}(\Omega). Calculus then gives us that

for all t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T].

Now suppose (1.6) has a unique global pseudo classical solution, u⁡(t)u(t). It follows that a pseudo classical solution of (1.1) exists for all T∈(0,∞)T\in(0,\infty), and uT​(t)=u​(t)u_{T}(t)=u(t) for all t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T]. This, in turn, allows us to conclude that

for all t∈(0,∞)t\in(0,\infty).

It is difficult to draw substantial conclusions from the above equation for general ff, but if ff is independent of time, we can say much more. We will now assume that ff does not depend on tt for the remainder of the section. Now note that if ff is independent of tt, (2.6) implies that

(2.7) m2​(u′​(t),u′​(t))L2+σ2​(u⁡(t),u⁡(t))H∗2+V⁡(u⁡(t))−(f,u⁡(t))L2=−(f,u⁡(0))L2+m2​(u′​(0),u′​(0))L2+σ2​(u⁡(0),u⁡(0))L2+V⁡(u⁡(0))−∫0t(F1(u′(s)),u′(s))L2ds.\begin{split}&\frac{m}{2}(u^{\prime}(t),u^{\prime}(t))_{L^{2}}+\frac{\sigma}{2}(u(t),u(t))_{H^{2}_{*}}+V(u(t))-(f,u(t))_{L^{2}}\\ &=-(f,u(0))_{L^{2}}+\frac{m}{2}(u^{\prime}(0),u^{\prime}(0))_{L^{2}}+\frac{\sigma}{2}(u(0),u(0))_{L^{2}}+V(u(0))\\ &-\int_{0}^{t}(F_{1}(u^{\prime}(s)),u^{\prime}(s))_{L^{2}}ds.\end{split}

Let us now turn our attention to finding two functionals that will be useful in the analysis of how solutions of (1.1) evolve with respect to time if ff is independent of time. Since this problem is motivated by a problem in continuum mechanics, previous experience suggests that we should look at the potential energy and the total energy. The former is

(2.8) ΣT​(u)=σ2​(u,u)H∗2+V⁡(u)−(f,u)L2.\Sigma_{T}(u)=\frac{\sigma}{2}(u,u)_{H^{2}_{*}}+V(u)-(f,u)_{L^{2}}.

The latter is

(2.9) Eu​(t)=m2​(u′​(t),u′​(t))L2+σ2​(u⁡(t),u⁡(t))H∗2+V⁡(u⁡(t))−(f,u⁡(t))L2.E_{u}(t)=\frac{m}{2}(u^{\prime}(t),u^{\prime}(t))_{L^{2}}+\frac{\sigma}{2}(u(t),u(t))_{H^{2}_{*}}+V(u(t))-(f,u(t))_{L^{2}}.

Notice that

(2.10) ΣT​ is coercive and bounded below on ​H∗2​(Ω).\Sigma_{T}\text{ is coercive and bounded below on }H^{2}_{*}(\Omega).

An immediate consequence of (2.7) is that

(2.11) Eu​ is non-increasing with respect to time,E_{u}\text{ is non-increasing with respect to time,}

and, in particular, Eu​(t)E_{u}(t) is bounded from above on [0,∞)[0,\infty). Combining this observation with (2.10) gives us that

(2.12) There exists a constant ​C​ such that ​(u⁡(t),u⁡(t))H∗2≤C​ for all ​t∈(0,∞).\text{There exists a constant }C\text{ such that }(u(t),u(t))_{H^{2}_{*}}\leq C\text{ for all }t\in(0,\infty).

Now, combining (2.7) with (2.10) we see that

(2.13) There exists a constant ​C​ such that ​∫0t(F1​(u′​(s)),u′​(s))L2​𝑑s≤C for all ​t∈(0,∞).\begin{split}&\text{There exists a constant }C\text{ such that }\int_{0}^{t}(F_{1}(u^{\prime}(s)),u^{\prime}(s))_{L^{2}}ds\leq C\\ &\text{ for all }t\in(0,\infty).\end{split}

Before we continue, let us make another observation about ΣT\Sigma_{T}. Note that if f2f_{2} is convex with a derivative that vanishes somehere on the real line, we can use the direct method of the calculus of variations to show that there exists a unique minimizer of ΣT\Sigma_{T} over H∗2​(Ω)H^{2}_{*}(\Omega). Furthermore, this minimizer will be the unique (weak) solution of the boundary value problem (1.7). Previous experience then suggests that if f2f_{2} is a convex function whose derivative vanishes somewhere then solutions of (1.1) should converge to the solution of (1.7) with respect to H∗2​(Ω)H^{2}_{*}(\Omega) norm as time goes to infinity. This is the subject of the next section.

Finally, we prove a result that will be useful in the next section.

Lemma 2.1.

Let f:[0,∞)→ℝf:[0,\infty)\rightarrow\mathbb{R} be a continuous non-negative function. Suppose as well that there exists a positive real number CC such that ∫0tf⁡(s)​𝑑s≤C\int_{0}^{t}f(s)ds\leq C for all t∈(0,∞)t\in(0,\infty). Then there exists a sequence {tn}n=1∞\{t_{n}\}_{n=1}^{\infty} with tn↑∞t_{n}\uparrow\infty such that ∫tntn+1f⁡(s)​𝑑s→0\int_{t_{n}}^{t_{n}+1}f(s)ds\rightarrow 0 as n→∞n\rightarrow\infty, and

(2.14) limn→∞[f⁡(tn)+f⁡(tn+1)]=0.\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}[f(t_{n})+f(t_{n}+1)]=0.
Proof.

Since ff is non-negative and since there exists a positive real number CC such that ∫0tf⁡(s)​𝑑s≤C\int_{0}^{t}f(s)ds\leq C for all t∈[0,∞)t\in[0,\infty), it follows that ∫2​n2​n+1f⁡(s)​𝑑s→0\int_{2n}^{2n+1}f(s)ds\rightarrow 0 as n→∞n\rightarrow\infty. Calculus then gives us that ∫2​n2​n+1f⁡(s+1)​𝑑s→0\int_{2n}^{2n+1}f(s+1)ds\rightarrow 0 as n→∞n\rightarrow\infty. It follows that

(2.15) ∫2​n2​n+1[f⁡(s)+f⁡(s+1)]​𝑑s→0​ as ​n→∞.\int_{2n}^{2n+1}[f(s)+f(s+1)]ds\rightarrow 0\text{ as }n\rightarrow\infty.

This in turn allows us to use the mean value theorem for integrals to conclude that there exists a sequence {tn}n=1∞\{t_{n}\}_{n=1}^{\infty} with tn∈(2​n,2​n+1)t_{n}\in(2n,2n+1) for all positive integers nn such that

(2.16) f⁡(tn)+f⁡(tn+1)→0​ as ​n→∞.f(t_{n})+f(t_{n}+1)\rightarrow 0\text{ as }n\rightarrow\infty.

Since ff is assumed to be non-negative we have that both f⁡(tn)f(t_{n}) and f⁡(tn+1)f(t_{n}+1) vanish as n→∞n\rightarrow\infty. Notice that we can also say that

(2.17) tn↑∞.t_{n}\uparrow\infty.

Now recall that ff is non-negative and that there exists a positive real number CC such that ∫0tf⁡(s)​𝑑s≤C\int_{0}^{t}f(s)ds\leq C for all t∈[0,∞)t\in[0,\infty). Note as well that the intersection of (2​m,2​m+2)(2m,2m+2) with (2​n,2​n+2)(2n,2n+2) is empty if mm and nn are positive integers with the property that m≠nm\neq n. It follows that

(2.18) ∫tntn+1f⁡(s)​𝑑s→0​ as ​n→∞.\int_{t_{n}}^{t_{n}+1}f(s)ds\rightarrow 0\text{ as }n\rightarrow\infty.

Combining (2.16) with (2.17) and (2.18), we see that we have the lemma.

3. Proof of Theorem 1.2

Proceeding as in [1] we argue as follows. First recall that we are assuming that a unique global pseudo classical solution uu to (1.6) exists. Now, note as well that the hypotheses of Theorem 1.1 give us that

(3.1) (F1​(u′​(t)),u′​(t))L2=c​‖u′​(t)‖L22+d​‖u′​(t)‖L33,(F_{1}(u^{\prime}(t)),u^{\prime}(t))_{L^{2}}=c||u^{\prime}(t)||_{L^{2}}^{2}+d||u^{\prime}(t)||_{L^{3}}^{3},

for all t∈(0,∞)t\in(0,\infty). We can now combine (2.13) with Lemma 2.1 to see that there is a sequence {tn}n=1∞\{t_{n}\}_{n=1}^{\infty} such that tn↑∞t_{n}\uparrow\infty,

(3.2) limn→∞∫tntn+1‖u′​(s)‖L22​𝑑s=0,\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\int_{t_{n}}^{t_{n}+1}||u^{\prime}(s)||_{L^{2}}^{2}ds=0,
(3.3) limn→∞∫tntn+1‖u′​(s)‖L33​𝑑s=0,\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\int_{t_{n}}^{t_{n}+1}||u^{\prime}(s)||_{L^{3}}^{3}ds=0,
(3.4) limn→∞(‖u′​(tn)‖L2+‖u′​(tn+1)‖L2)=0,\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}(||u^{\prime}(t_{n})||_{L^{2}}+||u^{\prime}(t_{n}+1)||_{L^{2}})=0,

and

(3.5) limn→∞(‖u′​(tn)‖L3+‖u′​(tn+1)‖L3)=0.\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}(||u^{\prime}(t_{n})||_{L^{3}}+||u^{\prime}(t_{n}+1)||_{L^{3}})=0.

Let v∈L2​((,,,))v\in L^{2}((a,b)), and notice that we also have that

(3.6) |∫tntn+1<u′′​(s),v>​ds|=|∫tntn+1(u′′​(s),v)L2​ds|=|(u′​(tn+1),v)L2−(u′​(tn),v)L2|≤|(u′​(tn+1),v)L2|+|(u′​(tn),v)L2|≤‖u′​(tn+1)‖L2​‖v‖L2+‖u′​(tn)‖L2||v||L2.\begin{split}|\int_{t_{n}}^{t_{n}+1}<u^{\prime\prime}(s),v>ds|&=|\int_{t_{n}}^{t_{n}+1}(u^{\prime\prime}(s),v)_{L^{2}}ds|\\ &=|(u^{\prime}(t_{n}+1),v)_{L^{2}}-(u^{\prime}(t_{n}),v)_{L^{2}}|\\ &\leq|(u^{\prime}(t_{n}+1),v)_{L^{2}}|+|(u^{\prime}(t_{n}),v)_{L^{2}}|\\ &\leq||u^{\prime}(t_{n}+1)||_{L^{2}}||v||_{L^{2}}+||u^{\prime}(t_{n})||_{L^{2}}||v||_{L^{2}}.\end{split}

Recalling (3.4), we see that the limit as nn goes to ∞\infty of ∫tntn+1<u′′​(s),v>​𝑑s\int_{t_{n}}^{t_{n}+1}<u^{\prime\prime}(s),v>ds is zero.

Now, let us bound another integral of a quantity that shows up in global pseudo classical solutions of (1.6). Suppose pp is a real number greater than or equal to 22 in value, suppose qq satisfies

(3.7) 1q+p−1p=1,\frac{1}{q}+\frac{p-1}{p}=1,

and note that

(3.8) |∫tntn+1(|u′​(s)|p−2​u′​(s),v)L2​ds|≤∫tntn+1‖u′​(s)‖Lpp−1​‖v‖Lq​𝑑s≤(∫tntn+1‖u′​(s)‖Lpp​ds)p−1p​(∫tntn+1‖v‖Lqq​ds)1q.\begin{split}&|\int_{t_{n}}^{t_{n}+1}(|u^{\prime}(s)|^{p-2}u^{\prime}(s),v)_{L^{2}}ds|\\ &\leq\int_{t_{n}}^{t_{n}+1}||u^{\prime}(s)||_{L^{p}}^{p-1}||v||_{L^{q}}ds\\ &\leq(\int_{t_{n}}^{t_{n}+1}||u^{\prime}(s)||_{L^{p}}^{p}ds)^{\frac{p-1}{p}}(\int_{t_{n}}^{t_{n}+1}||v||_{L^{q}}^{q}ds)^{\frac{1}{q}}.\end{split}

We can now use (3.2) and (3.3) to conclude that the right hand side of the last inequality above vanishes as n→∞n\rightarrow\infty, provided that p∈{2,3}p\in\{2,3\}. We can now use the mean value theorem for integrals to conclude that for all v∈H∗2​(Ω)v\in H^{2}_{*}(\Omega) there exists a sequence {tnv}n=1∞\{t_{n}^{v}\}_{n=1}^{\infty} with tnv∈(tn,tn+1)t^{v}_{n}\in(t_{n},t_{n}+1) for all nn such that

(3.9) limn→∞[m⁡<u′′​(tnv),v>+c​(u′​(tnv),v)L2+d​(|u′​(tnv)|​u′​(tnv),v)L2]=0.\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}[m<u^{\prime\prime}(t^{v}_{n}),v>+c(u^{\prime}(t^{v}_{n}),v)_{L^{2}}+d(|u^{\prime}(t^{v}_{n})|u^{\prime}(t^{v}_{n}),v)_{L^{2}}]=0.

Now fix v∈H∗2​(Ω)v\in H^{2}_{*}(\Omega) and recall that ‖u⁡(t)‖H∗2||u(t)||_{H^{2}_{*}} is bounded independent of tt. It follows that there exists a function u^v∈H∗2​(Ω)\hat{u}_{v}\in H^{2}_{*}(\Omega) such that

(3.10) u⁡(tnv)⇀u^v∈H∗2​(Ω)u(t^{v}_{n})\rightharpoonup\hat{u}_{v}\in H^{2}_{*}(\Omega)

up to a subsequence. By compactness we have u⁡(tnv)→u^vu(t^{v}_{n})\rightarrow\hat{u}_{v} in L2​(Ω)L^{2}(\Omega). Now take a function w≠vw\neq v and consider {tnw}n=1∞\{t^{w}_{n}\}_{n=1}^{\infty}. Then u⁡(tnw)→u^wu(t^{w}_{n})\rightarrow\hat{u}_{w} in L2​(Ω)L^{2}(\Omega), and u⁡(tnw)⇀u^wu(t^{w}_{n})\rightharpoonup\hat{u}_{w} in H∗2​(Ω)H^{2}_{*}(\Omega). By (3.2), Hölder’s inequality, and the Fubini-Tonelli Theorem we obtain

(3.11) ‖u⁡(tnv)−u⁡(tnw)‖L22=∫Ω|∫tnvtnwu′​(s)​𝑑s|2​𝑑x≤∫Ω(∫tnvtnw|u′|2​𝑑s)​(|tnw−tnv|)​𝑑x≤|tnw−tnv|​∫tnvtnw‖u′​(s)‖L22​𝑑s≤∫tntn+1‖u′​(s)‖L22​ds→0\begin{split}||u(t^{v}_{n})-u(t^{w}_{n})||_{L^{2}}^{2}&=\int_{\Omega}|\int_{t^{v}_{n}}^{t^{w}_{n}}u^{\prime}(s)ds|^{2}dx\\ &\leq\int_{\Omega}(\int_{t^{v}_{n}}^{t^{w}_{n}}|u^{\prime}|^{2}ds)(|t^{w}_{n}-t^{v}_{n}|)dx\\ &\leq|t^{w}_{n}-t^{v}_{n}|\int_{t^{v}_{n}}^{t^{w}_{n}}||u^{\prime}(s)||_{L^{2}}^{2}ds\\ &\leq\int_{t_{n}}^{t_{n}+1}||u^{\prime}(s)||_{L^{2}}^{2}ds\rightarrow 0\end{split}

as n→∞n\rightarrow\infty. This shows that the limit u^v\hat{u}_{v} is independent of vv, so let’s call it u^\hat{u}. At this point, we have showed that for all v∈H∗2​(Ω)v\in H^{2}_{*}(\Omega)

(3.12) σ​(u^,v)H∗2+(F2​(u^),v)L2−(f,v)L2=limn→∞[m<u′′(tvn),v>+c(u′(tvn),v)L2+d(|u′(tvn)|u′(tvn),v)L2+σ(u(tvn),v)H∗2+(F2(u(tvn)),v)L2−(f,v)L2]=0.\begin{split}&\sigma(\hat{u},v)_{H^{2}_{*}}+(F_{2}(\hat{u}),v)_{L^{2}}-(f,v)_{L^{2}}\\ &=\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}[m<u^{\prime\prime}(t^{v}_{n}),v>+c(u^{\prime}(t^{v}_{n}),v)_{L^{2}}+d(|u^{\prime}(t^{v}_{n})|u^{\prime}(t^{v}_{n}),v)_{L^{2}}\\ &+\sigma(u(t^{v}_{n}),v)_{H^{2}_{*}}+(F_{2}(u(t^{v}_{n})),v)_{L^{2}}-(f,v)_{L^{2}}]\\ &=0.\end{split}

This shows that u^\hat{u} is the unique solution to (1.7). Now, subtracting the Euler-Lagrange equation contained in (1.7) from the equation of motion contained in (1.6), we see that for all v∈H∗2​(Ω)v\in H^{2}_{*}(\Omega)

(3.13) <u′′​(t),v>+c​(u′​(t),v)L2+d​(|u′​(t)|​u′​(t),v)L2+(u⁡(t)−u^,v)H∗2+(F2​(u⁡(t))−F2​(u^),v)L2=0\begin{split}&<u^{\prime\prime}(t),v>+c(u^{\prime}(t),v)_{L^{2}}+d(|u^{\prime}(t)|u^{\prime}(t),v)_{L^{2}}+(u(t)-\hat{u},v)_{H^{2}_{*}}\\ &+(F_{2}(u(t))-F_{2}(\hat{u}),v)_{L^{2}}=0\ \end{split}

for all t∈(0,∞)t\in(0,\infty). This in turn allows us to write

(3.14) ∫tntn+1[<u′′(s),u(s)−u^>+c(u′(s),u(s)−u^)L2+d​(|u′​(s)|​u′​(s),u⁡(s)−u^)L2+(u⁡(s)−u^,u⁡(s)−u^)H∗2+(F2(u(s))−F2(u^),u(s)−u^)L2]ds=0\begin{split}&\int_{t_{n}}^{t_{n}+1}[<u^{\prime\prime}(s),u(s)-\hat{u}>+c(u^{\prime}(s),u(s)-\hat{u})_{L^{2}}\\ &+d(|u^{\prime}(s)|u^{\prime}(s),u(s)-\hat{u})_{L^{2}}+(u(s)-\hat{u},u(s)-\hat{u})_{H^{2}_{*}}\\ &+(F_{2}(u(s))-F_{2}(\hat{u}),u(s)-\hat{u})_{L^{2}}]ds=0\end{split}

for all positive integers nn.

Now, let us investigate the limiting behavior of the terms on the left hand side of the above equation. Let pp be a real number greater than or equal to 22 in value, and let 1q+p−1p=1\frac{1}{q}+\frac{p-1}{p}=1, then we have

(3.15) |∫tntn+1(|u′​(s)|p−2​u′​(s),u⁡(s)−u^)L2​ds|≤∫tntn+1‖u′​(s)‖Lpp−1||u⁡(s)−u^||Lq​𝑑s≤C​∫tntn+1‖u′​(s)‖Lpp−1​𝑑s≤C​(∫tntn+1‖u′​(s)‖Lpp​ds)p−1p.\begin{split}|\int_{t_{n}}^{t_{n}+1}(|u^{\prime}(s)|^{p-2}u^{\prime}(s),u(s)-\hat{u})_{L^{2}}ds|&\leq\int_{t_{n}}^{t_{n}+1}||u^{\prime}(s)||_{L^{p}}^{p-1}||u(s)-\hat{u}||_{L^{q}}ds\\ &\leq C\int_{t_{n}}^{t_{n}+1}||u^{\prime}(s)||_{L^{p}}^{p-1}ds\\ &\leq C(\int_{t_{n}}^{t_{n}+1}||u^{\prime}(s)||_{L^{p}}^{p}ds)^{\frac{p-1}{p}}.\end{split}

The quantity on the right hand side of the last inequality above vanishes as n→∞n\rightarrow\infty, if p∈{2,3}p\in\{2,3\}. Here, and for the remainder of the proof, CC will denote a constant that is independent of nn and that can change value from line to line. Note, we used (2.12) to obtain a uniform bound on ‖u⁡(t)−u^‖Lq||u(t)-\hat{u}||_{L^{q}}.

We also have that

(3.16) |∫tntn+1<u′′(s),u(s)−u^>ds|=|∫tntn+1(u′′​(s),u⁡(s)−u^)L2​ds|≤|∫tntn+1(u′​(s),u′​(s))L2​ds|+|(u′​(t),u⁡(t)−u^)L2|tntn+1|≤∫tntn+1‖u′​(s)‖22​ds+C⁡(‖u′​(tn+1)‖L2+||u′​(tn)||L2)→0\begin{split}&|\int_{t_{n}}^{t_{n}+1}<u^{\prime\prime}(s),u(s)-\hat{u}>ds|\\ &=|\int_{t_{n}}^{t_{n}+1}(u^{\prime\prime}(s),u(s)-\hat{u})_{L^{2}}ds|\\ &\leq|\int_{t_{n}}^{t_{n}+1}(u^{\prime}(s),u^{\prime}(s))_{L^{2}}ds|+|(u^{\prime}(t),u(t)-\hat{u})_{L^{2}}|_{t_{n}}^{t_{n}+1}|\\ &\leq\int_{t_{n}}^{t_{n}+1}||u^{\prime}(s)||_{2}^{2}ds+C(||u^{\prime}(t_{n}+1)||_{L^{2}}+||u^{\prime}(t_{n})||_{L^{2}})\\ &\rightarrow 0\end{split}

as n→∞n\rightarrow\infty. Here we used (2.12) to obtain a uniform bound on ‖u⁡(t)−u^‖L2||u(t)-\hat{u}||_{L^{2}}.

Now, since F2F_{2} is a non-decreasing function we also have that

(3.17) (F2​(u⁡(t))−F2​(u^),u⁡(t)−u^)≥0(F_{2}(u(t))-F_{2}(\hat{u}),u(t)-\hat{u})\geq 0

for all t∈(0,∞)t\in(0,\infty). We can now use (3.14) to conclude that

(3.18) ∫tntn+1‖u⁡(s)−u^‖H∗22​𝑑s→0​ as ​n→∞.\int_{t_{n}}^{t_{n}+1}||u(s)-\hat{u}||_{H^{2}_{*}}^{2}ds\rightarrow 0\text{ as }n\rightarrow\infty.

Now, recalling (3.2), we have

(3.19) ∫tntn+1(‖u⁡(s)−u^‖H∗22+‖u′​(s)‖L22)​𝑑s→0​ as ​n→∞\int_{t_{n}}^{t_{n}+1}(||u(s)-\hat{u}||_{H^{2}_{*}}^{2}+||u^{\prime}(s)||_{L^{2}}^{2})ds\rightarrow 0\text{ as }n\rightarrow\infty

and hence we can use the mean value theorem for integrals to conclude that there exists a t¯n∈[tn,tn+1]\bar{t}_{n}\in[t_{n},t_{n}+1] for all positive integers nn such that

This, in turn, implies that

(3.21) limn→∞Eu​(t¯n)=ΣT​(u^)=I:=minv∈H∗2​(Ω)⁡ΣT​(v).\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}E_{u}(\bar{t}_{n})=\Sigma_{T}(\hat{u})=I:=\min_{v\in H^{2}_{*}(\Omega)}\Sigma_{T}(v).

But Eu​(t¯n)E_{u}(\bar{t}_{n}) is decreasing so that we have

(3.22) limt→∞Eu​(t)=I.\lim_{t\rightarrow\infty}E_{u}(t)=I.

Now recall from section two that Eu​(t)=12​‖u′​(t)‖L22+ΣT​(u⁡(t))E_{u}(t)=\frac{1}{2}||u^{\prime}(t)||_{L^{2}}^{2}+\Sigma_{T}(u(t)). From this it follows that Eu​(t)≥12​‖u′​(t)‖L22+IE_{u}(t)\geq\frac{1}{2}||u^{\prime}(t)||_{L^{2}}^{2}+I. Passing to the limit as t→∞t\rightarrow\infty we see that

(3.23) I=limt→∞Eu​(t)≥I+lim supt→∞12​‖u′​(t)‖L22.I=\lim_{t\rightarrow\infty}E_{u}(t)\geq I+\limsup_{t\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{2}||u^{\prime}(t)||_{L^{2}}^{2}.

The above allow us to conclude that u′​(t)→0u^{\prime}(t)\rightarrow 0 as t→∞t\rightarrow\infty. This, in turn, allows us to write

(3.24) limt→∞ΣT​(u⁡(t))=limt→∞Eu​(t)−limt→∞12​‖u′​(t)‖L22=I=ΣT​(u^).\lim_{t\rightarrow\infty}\Sigma_{T}(u(t))=\lim_{t\rightarrow\infty}E_{u}(t)-\lim_{t\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{2}||u^{\prime}(t)||_{L^{2}}^{2}=I=\Sigma_{T}(\hat{u}).

It follows that u⁡(t)→u^u(t)\rightarrow\hat{u} in H∗2​(Ω)H^{2}_{*}(\Omega) on the whole flow. Theorem 1.2 follows.
